subtopics.title: Cauvery River and its basin
subtopics.summary: The Cauvery is an east-flowing Peninsular River, known as 'Ganga of the South', that rises at Talakaveri in Kodagu, Karnataka. It flows through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu before draining into the Bay of Bengal near Poompuhar. Its drainage basin covers four states and UTs, and its upper and lower basins receive different monsoons.

subtopics.title: Historical roots and tribunal awards
subtopics.summary: The dispute has roots in an 1892 agreement between the Madras Presidency and the princely state of Mysore, after which Madras objected to Mysore's irrigation and storage plans. A 1924 agreement allowed Mysore to build a dam at Kannambadi, which led to the Krishnaraja Sagar Dam. After the agreement came up for review following 1974, the matter moved to the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, constituted in 1990, whose 2007 award and the 2018 Supreme Court judgment fixed the water shares.

subtopics.title: Cauvery Water Management Authority
subtopics.summary: The Cauvery Water Management Authority was established in 2018 under the Cauvery Water Management Scheme, 2018, along with the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee. It is a statutory, quasi-judicial body notified under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, and its purpose is to implement the modified CWDT Award upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018. Its composition mixes full-time members, part-time central government members and part-time members from the basin states, with headquarters in New Delhi under the Ministry of Jal Shakti.

subtopics.title: Mekedatu project and the latest order
subtopics.summary: The Cauvery Water Management Authority endorsed an order directing Karnataka to release 3,500 Cusecs (around 4.5 TMC ft) of Cauvery water to Tamil Nadu. Tamil Nadu has opposed Karnataka's proposed Mekedatu Balancing Reservoir Project, which aims to supply drinking water to Bengaluru and generate approximately 400 MW of power. Tamil Nadu raised objections to the project in 2018 and approached the Supreme Court.

quizzes.passage: The Cauvery water dispute is one of the oldest inter-state water conflicts in India, and its roots lie in agreements made long before independence. The disagreement began between the Madras Presidency and the princely state of Mysore. Madras objected when Mysore planned to expand its irrigation and build new water storage structures on the river. A later arrangement allowed Mysore to construct a dam at a village in the region, and that dam later became a major reservoir. The original agreement was meant to operate for a fixed period, and when it came up for review, it became a major source of contention between the successor states. The upper riparian state wants more water for Bengaluru's drinking water and irrigation, while the lower riparian state wants assured releases to support the agriculture of its delta. Because the states could not settle the matter by agreement, the dispute was taken up under the legal framework available for such conflicts. A tribunal was then formed to decide the sharing of water, and its award was later examined by the Supreme Court. Today, a statutory body works to put the final decision into practice, with the help of a regulation committee. Current releases and new projects such as Mekedatu keep the dispute active in public debate.

quizzes.passage: Implementing a river water award requires a permanent institution, and for the Cauvery the government set up a dedicated authority. The body was created together with a regulation committee, so that management and monitoring work could be divided. Its legal character is that of a statutory and quasi-judicial body, which means it has a legal basis in a central law on inter-state river disputes. Its main job is to give effect to the modified tribunal award, which the country's highest court had upheld. The authority is headed by a senior official who serves for a fixed term, and it includes full-time and part-time members. Members come from the basin states and a union territory as well as from the central government, so that all stakeholders have a voice in decisions. The authority's functions include ensuring that water is released as directed, which makes its work closely watched by the states. Its work has come into sharp focus recently, after it endorsed an order on water releases from one state to another. Understanding its composition and legal status helps explain how the Cauvery dispute is managed today. Because its decisions affect farmers and cities alike, the authority plays a central role in the dispute.
